audit_items.title: Does trie_get correctly return the value set by trie_set, and return trie.default for unset keys?
audit_items.state_context: dirtyFields map[types.FieldIndex]bool; merkleLayers [][][]byte; b.lock sync.RWMutex. Setters call markFieldAsDirty; HashTreeRoot calls recomputeDirtyFields to flush dirty leaves into the Merkle tree.

phase1.summary: The EL trie_get/trie_set consistency concept (read-after-write in a Patricia trie) does not exist in Prysm (a CL client). The CL analog is the dirtyFields + merkleLayers lazy Merkle cache. Every setter calls markFieldAsDirty(field); HashTreeRoot acquires b.lock.Lock() and calls recomputeDirtyFields before returning the root. This ensures all prior writes are reflected in the returned root.
state_anomalies: Staleness window between setter call and next HashTreeRoot: merkleLayers[0][idx] is stale until recomputed. This is by design.
recomputeDirtyFields iterates over b.dirtyFields while deleting from it — safe in Go, and the full b.lock.Lock() prevents concurrent modification.
Direct mutation of proto pointer fields obtained via getters bypasses the setter pattern and dirty marking — not exploitable externally.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: HashTreeRoot holds b.lock.Lock() for full duration, serializing all concurrent setter and Copy() access. No exploitable race condition found.

phase2.summary: Tracing the read-after-write concrete path: SetSlot(x) → markFieldAsDirty(Slot) → HashTreeRoot() → recomputeDirtyFields() computes correct root. No counterexample found.
phase2.counterexample: None — the dirty-field system correctly ensures all writes are reflected in the next HashTreeRoot.
attack_scenarios: Scenario (proto pointer bypass): b.fork.CurrentVersion = X directly modifies a proto field without triggering markFieldAsDirty. HashTreeRoot would return a stale fork root until something else marks Fork dirty. Not externally triggerable — requires internal code access.

phase2_5.attack_surface: Read-after-write consistency of the Merkle cache is enforced correctly through the dirty-field system for the documented API contract.

phase3.summary: Invariant 'HashTreeRoot returns a root reflecting all prior setter calls' holds. dirtyFields + b.lock.Lock() are sufficient guards for all externally-triggered state mutations.
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for externally-triggered mutations. Proto-pointer bypass is a design limitation not externally exploitable.

phase3_5.reason: PROP-0004 describes EL Patricia Trie trie_get/trie_set consistency. These functions do not exist in Prysm (CL). The CL analog (dirty-field Merkle cache consistency) is correctly implemented. No vulnerability found.
phase3_5.recommendation: None required. The CL Merkle cache invariant is upheld.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Are all keys in secured tries properly hashed with keccak256 before storage in the prepared trie mapping?
audit_items.state_context: SSZ Merkle tree uses compile-time constant field positions (types.FieldIndex enum) as leaf indices. No attacker-controlled key insertion.

phase1.summary: The EL 'secured trie' concept (keccak256 key hashing to prevent trie-balancing attacks) is architecturally absent in Prysm's CL. The CL SSZ Merkle tree uses compile-time constant field positions (types.FieldIndex.RealPosition()) as leaf indices — there is no attacker-controlled key insertion. The concept of trie-balancing attacks does not apply.
state_anomalies: fieldMap maps FieldIndex constants to DataType; new fork fields must be added explicitly — but this is a developer concern, not an attacker-controlled path.
No analog to keccak256 key hashing: leaf positions are fixed uint constants.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: fieldMap is read-only after init(); no concurrent modification risk.

phase2.summary: No attacker-controlled key in the CL Merkle tree construction. Field positions are enum constants set at compile time. An attacker cannot influence which leaf position a field maps to.
phase2.counterexample: None — attacker-controlled key hashing is an EL-only concern.
attack_scenarios: Scenario (validator index edge-case): Attacker sends a beacon block with validators at max index. handleValidatorMVSlice validates idx > uint64(totalLen)-1 and returns an error. No trie-balancing is possible.

phase2_5.attack_surface: No attack surface for trie-balancing in SSZ position-indexed Merkle trees.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'keys are hashed before storage' does not apply to the CL SSZ Merkle tree. The CL invariant 'field positions are fixed compile-time constants' holds trivially.
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Compile-time field position constants (types.FieldIndex enum) are fully sufficient.

phase3_5.reason: PROP-0005 describes an EL patricia trie concern (keccak256 key hashing in secured tries). This concept is architecturally absent in Prysm's SSZ-based CL state. No CL analog vulnerability exists.
phase3_5.recommendation: Redirect this property to EL client audit.

audit_items.title: Can encode_node produce empty bytes (b'') for any valid input, violating the non-empty encoding invariant?
audit_items.state_context: ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher allocates fieldRoots as make([][]byte, fieldCount) — nil-initialized — then populates each slot via version-gated branches. Merkleize() pads nil entries with 32-byte zero slices rather than returning an error.

phase1.summary: The EL encode_node non-empty bytes invariant maps in CL to: all field root slots in ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher must be non-nil 32-byte values after the function returns. The risk is: if a new fork field is added to fuluFields but ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher is not updated, the corresponding slot remains nil. Merkleize() silently treats nil as a zero-hash leaf rather than raising an error.
state_anomalies: ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher allocates fieldRoots = make([][]byte, fieldCount) — nil-initialized. Unpopulated slots remain nil.
Merkleize() in stateutil/trie_helpers.go pads with make([]byte, 32) (zero-filled) for nil entries — silent wrong root rather than an error.
For all currently deployed fork versions (Phase0 through Fulu), all slots are correctly populated by the version-gated branches.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher is called inside b.lock.Lock() — state fields are stable during computation.

phase2.summary: No nil-root scenario exists for currently deployed versions (Phase0-Fulu). The gap would appear only if a new fork's fields were added to the field list without updating the hasher — a developer-level bug, not externally exploitable.
attack_scenarios: Scenario (nil root on new fork): Future fork X adds field Y. State initializer adds Y to fuluFields, but ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher is not updated. InitializeMerkleLayers calls ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher, gets nil for Y's position, Merkleize() pads with zeros. State root differs from other clients. Causes consensus split. NOT externally triggerable — requires developer error.

entry_points: Internal code path only (developer omission in new fork)
phase2_5.attack_surface: Only reachable if a developer forgets to add a new fork's field to ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher. Not externally triggerable.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'all field roots are non-nil 32-byte values' holds for all currently deployed fork versions. The Merkleize() zero-padding is a design weakness — it masks missing fields rather than failing loudly.
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for current code. The zero-padding defense is incomplete — it masks missing fields rather than failing loudly. Should be addressed as a hardening measure.
edge_cases: Future fork compatibility: Adding a new field to the fork field list without updating ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher produces a silent wrong state root.

phase3_5.reason: PROP-0006 describes an EL encode_node empty-bytes concern. The CL analog (nil SSZ field root via missing-field bug) is not currently exploitable for deployed code. The silent zero-padding design weakness is a hardening concern only.
phase3_5.recommendation: Add an assertion in ComputeFieldRootsWithHasher that all slots in fieldRoots are non-nil after population. This ensures missing-field bugs in new forks are caught loudly rather than producing silent wrong state roots.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does encode_node for Account values always receive and use a valid (non-None) storage root from get_storage_root callback?
audit_items.state_context: BeaconState struct has three execution payload header fields: latestExecutionPayloadHeader (*enginev1.ExecutionPayloadHeader, Bellatrix), latestExecutionPayloadHeaderCapella (*enginev1.ExecutionPayloadHeaderCapella, Capella), latestExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb (*enginev1.ExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb, Deneb/Electra/Fulu). All stored as pointers; nil is a valid Go pointer value. InitializeFromProtoUnsafe* variants assign directly from proto fields without nil checks.

phase1.summary: The EL encode_node nil-storage-root concept maps in CL to: latestExecutionPayloadHeader* fields in BeaconState can be nil if the protobuf input contains nil execution payload headers. The CL initializers (InitializeFromProtoUnsafe*) store nil without checking. rootSelector calls .HashTreeRoot() and Copy() calls .Copy() on these potentially-nil pointer fields — causing nil pointer dereference panics (DoS).
state_anomalies: InitializeFromProtoUnsafeBellatrix: latestExecutionPayloadHeader = st.LatestExecutionPayloadHeader — no nil check. If proto input has nil header, field is nil.
rootSelector at line ~1147 calls b.latestExecutionPayloadHeader.HashTreeRoot() — nil pointer dereference if field is nil.
Copy() at lines ~806-808 calls b.latestExecutionPayloadHeader.Copy(), b.latestExecutionPayloadHeaderCapella.Copy(), b.latestExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb.Copy() — all panic if nil.
The 'safe' initializers (InitializeFromProto*) call proto.Clone() but proto.Clone of a message with nil submessage fields leaves those fields nil.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: nil pointer dereference is a logic bug; locking does not prevent it.

phase2.summary: Concrete exploit: call InitializeFromProtoUnsafeBellatrix(proto) where proto.LatestExecutionPayloadHeader = nil, then call state.HashTreeRoot(). Panics at rootSelector with nil pointer dereference.
phase2.counterexample: InitializeFromProtoUnsafeBellatrix(&ethpb.BeaconStateBellatrix{LatestExecutionPayloadHeader: nil}) → stores nil in latestExecutionPayloadHeader → state.HashTreeRoot() → rootSelector → b.latestExecutionPayloadHeader.HashTreeRoot() → PANIC: nil pointer dereference.
attack_scenarios: Scenario A (malicious state import via checkpoint sync): Attacker delivers a BeaconStateBellatrix protobuf with LatestExecutionPayloadHeader = nil to a node performing checkpoint sync. Node creates a BeaconState with nil latestExecutionPayloadHeader. When HashTreeRoot is called during block processing, the node panics — DoS.
Scenario B (database corruption): Corrupt database entry with nil execution payload header causes panic on startup during state root verification.
Scenario C (Copy panic): Any code path that calls Copy() on a Bellatrix/Capella/Deneb/Electra/Fulu state with nil execution payload header also panics.

phase2_5.attack_surface: Requires delivering or inducing a nil LatestExecutionPayloadHeader in a Bellatrix+ state. Upstream validation in the sync/import pipeline may independently reject nil payload headers — but the absence of a local nil guard in safety-critical functions is a defense-in-depth gap.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'latestExecutionPayloadHeader* is non-nil for Bellatrix+ states' is ASSUMED but not enforced locally. No nil check in InitializeFromProtoUnsafe* or in rootSelector/Copy(). Guard relies entirely on upstream validation being correct and complete.
phase3.guard_identified: Upstream state validation (assumed to reject nil payload headers)
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Insufficient at this code level. Local nil guards are absent from safety-critical functions (HashTreeRoot, Copy). Defense relies entirely on upstream validation.

phase3_5.reason: Nil execution payload header in Bellatrix/Capella/Deneb/Electra/Fulu state causes a node panic (DoS) in HashTreeRoot() and Copy(). The initializer stores nil without checking. The panic is reachable from state import paths (checkpoint sync, database load). While upstream validation is expected to prevent this, the absence of a local nil guard creates a defense-in-depth gap that could be exploited if upstream validation has any bypass.
phase3_5.severity_estimate: Medium — DoS via nil pointer panic in state processing
phase3_5.recommendation: Add nil checks for latestExecutionPayloadHeader*, latestExecutionPayloadHeaderCapella*, and latestExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb* in all InitializeFromProtoUnsafe* functions. Alternatively, initialize nil proto submessage fields to empty structs rather than nil. Also add nil guards in rootSelector and Copy() before calling .HashTreeRoot() and .Copy() on these fields.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does get_storage_root callback return the correct, canonical 32-byte storage root for each address?
audit_items.state_context: BeaconState.latestExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb stores Electra and Fulu execution payload headers using the Deneb-typed proto (*enginev1.ExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb). Verified: electra.proto defines no new ExecutionPayloadHeader type; fulu.proto defines no new ExecutionPayloadHeader type. specrefs/containers.yml shows Electra/Fulu BeaconState use same ExecutionPayloadHeader schema as Deneb. Execution requests (EIP-6110, EIP-7002, EIP-7251) are tracked separately in the beacon state, not in the execution payload header.

phase1.summary: The EL get_storage_root canonical-root concept maps in CL to: does latestExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb.HashTreeRoot() return the canonical 32-byte root for the execution payload header, even for Electra and Fulu states? Analysis: Electra and Fulu reuse the Deneb execution payload header schema. The proto investigation confirms no ExecutionPayloadHeaderElectra or ExecutionPayloadHeaderFulu types exist. The spec reference (specrefs/containers.yml) confirms BeaconState#electra and #fulu use the same ExecutionPayloadHeader schema as Deneb.
state_anomalies: Initial concern: Electra/Fulu using *enginev1.ExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb — potential schema mismatch if new fields were introduced.

Resolution: Verified via proto inspection. electra.proto and fulu.proto define NO new ExecutionPayloadHeader types. New Electra/Fulu data (execution requests, proposer lookahead) is stored as separate beacon state fields, not in the execution payload header.
The BeaconState struct and proto definitions are internally consistent for Electra and Fulu.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: No concurrency concerns specific to this field — rootSelector is called under b.lock.Lock().

phase2.summary: The initially-suspected type mismatch (Electra/Fulu payload header stored in Deneb-typed field) is confirmed to be correct-by-design: the Electra and Fulu forks did not change the execution payload header SSZ schema. Execution requests are tracked as separate beacon state fields. No schema mismatch exists.
phase2.counterexample: None — the Deneb execution payload header schema is intentionally reused for Electra and Fulu.
attack_scenarios: No attack scenario identified. The schema reuse is correct per the fork specifications.

phase2_5.attack_surface: No attack surface identified. The Deneb execution payload header schema is canonical for Electra and Fulu in this implementation.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'latestExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb.HashTreeRoot() returns the canonical 32-byte root for Electra/Fulu payload headers' holds. Verified: Electra/Fulu use the same execution payload header schema as Deneb (no new fields added at these fork boundaries per the spec and proto definitions).
phase3.guard_identified: SSZ deterministic hash computation via fastssz-generated HashTreeRoot on ExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Fully sufficient. Schema is correct for Electra and Fulu.

phase3_5.reason: PROP-0008 describes an EL get_storage_root canonical root concern. The CL analog (execution payload header root correctness for Electra/Fulu) was investigated. Confirmed: the Deneb-typed execution payload header is correctly reused for Electra and Fulu because the schema did not change at those fork boundaries. Execution requests (new in Electra) are tracked as separate beacon state fields, not in the payload header. No vulnerability found.
phase3_5.recommendation: None required. The field type naming (ExecutionPayloadHeaderDeneb for Electra/Fulu states) could benefit from a clarifying comment to prevent future confusion.
